title: Shiva's blue throat
carry: shiva swallows the poison so the world can live
tomorrow: a cow, a horse, a goddess rise from the sea. real, or a picture?

cards: Look closely at a picture of Shiva and there's a strange detail at his throat: it's blue. Not his face, his throat. The answer is in the churning.

The gods and asuras are pulling, the tortoise is holding, the sea is foaming, and the first thing to rise out of the ocean of milk isn't nectar. It's halahala, a poison so fierce the world starts to burn.

teach.b: No one planned for this. They came for amrita, and the sea gave them poison first. The gods and asuras can't handle it, and they don't pretend they can.
They go to Shiva and ask for help. In the Bhagavata Purana's telling, Shiva turns to Parvati first and says what power is for: protecting those who can't protect themselves.
Then he takes the poison in his hand and drinks it, out of compassion for everyone suffering. It doesn't kill him.
It stays in his throat and turns it dark blue, and so one of his names is Nilakantha, the blue-throated one. In some tellings, Parvati presses his throat so the poison goes no further.
So the puzzle is solved: the blue is the mark of a god who took the world's poison into himself so it wouldn't burn.
And this is why you'll see devotees pouring water and milk over the Shiva linga, especially on Mondays and through the month of Shravan.
Many say it cools the throat that still holds the poison. Hindus don't picture Shiva above the world's pain. They picture him holding it.
And the tortoise is still underneath; the story keeps its order: poison first, treasures after.

how: Shiva is shown with a blue throat and honored as Nilakantha; devotees pour water and milk over the Shiva linga, especially on Mondays and in the month of Shravan, and many say it cools the poison he holds.

games.q: a friend sees a Shiva statue with a blue throat and says 'so he's the poison god?' fairest reply?
o: no: he drank the poison so the world wouldn't burn. the blue is that.
yes: he rules over poisons and sickness.
it's just how artists color him; there's no story.
games.why: Shiva drank the halahala out of compassion, and it stayed in his throat. that's why he's Nilakantha, and why many devotees pour cooling water over the linga.

practice: If you have water nearby, pour a little slowly, over a plant or into a bowl, the way devotees pour it over the Shiva linga. As it pours, name one hard thing that's come up lately, in a few plain words.
Then breathe slowly for the rest of the sit. If you pray, you can offer it to Shiva, or simply to God; if you don't, just watch the water fall.

wordCard.voice: Kurma: the tortoise who keeps holding, even when the churning brings up poison first.

orig.note: Sanskrit Nilakantha, the blue-throated one: Shiva's name from the churning.
